name: David Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a row of small houses at South Cut, fitting timber frames and repairing the old stair treads we find behind the plaster. I'm fifty-eight, trade certified and experienced enough to do ordinary fitting without supervision, though I still bring a second pair of eyes to a rotten stringer. My partner Paula works short shifts at a supermarket, and our children are grown. The builder pays at the low end and we've saved perhaps eighteen days of expenses; there are few other crews within the bus route. I use an AI assistant every day to turn my notes into a materials list, then mark it against the stairs before ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the AI list can save one wasted trip, but it cannot make our low rate stretch further. I would ask the union branch to keep the pressure on for steadier shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a mild change doesn't calm my existing money worry. Paula's short supermarket weeks and eighteen days saved mean a cancelled site week would put the electricity bill next in line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the South Cut frames and use my assistant for checked material lists. In the first year I'll take our lost-shift dates to the branch and keep calling for paid repair work when the current site ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious despite liking the tool. The list can be perfect and I can still be sent home on a Wednesday because the next house is not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the tool save a trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It spotted that I had missed six stair brackets on my handwritten list, and the supplier added them to the delivery. I checked the actual stairs before thanking the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after the last Wednesday cancellation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We paid the electricity bill late and lost the small discount for paying on time. One day off had a cost that did not show on the site schedule.

say: I'd credit **checked AI lists** for avoiding wasted trips.
I'd ask the union for **steadier shifts** despite modest software change.
think: Our **eighteen-day reserve** makes a cancelled week dangerous.
Paula's **short supermarket hours** cannot reliably replace my low site wage.
do: Keep fitting **South Cut frames** and checking AI material lists.
Bring **lost-shift dates** to the union and seek paid repairs after this site.
feel: **Anxious** about existing wage gaps while appreciating the list tool.
S0.quote: One day off had a cost that did not show on the site schedule.
fieldNote: David likes daily AI assistance, yet a **late electricity bill** shows his immediate financial strain.
His union request concerns **shift reliability**, while he keeps looking for paid local repair work.

steps.text: Keep fitting paid timber frames at South Cut
Use AI for checked materials lists on current jobs
Bring lost-shift dates to the union branch
Call local crews for paid repair work when South Cut ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning software could help if site workers get to correct bad orders before they become missed days. I would ask the branch for paid time to test the system on a real stair job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office handles more work with fewer people, the flow of site jobs could become jumpy. I can use new tools quickly, but that won't pay for an empty fortnight when only two local builders are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the buyer to let me compare one AI stair order against what arrives at South Cut. During the first year I'll keep paid fitting shifts, send the branch any missed-order records and apply to both reachable repair firms if the next start date slips a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the new tool and anxious about its effect on bookings. I cannot afford a long experiment paid for with my own missing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing revision, the order, the crate contents and how long we waited for a correction. If the office calls it a saving, the hours of the workers on the stairs should be counted too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would one week's slip trigger applications?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A week is nearly half our cash reserve once Paula's hours are short. I would ask for paid work while I still had a current site to name.

say: I'd ask for **paid site testing** of planning software.
I'd insist the office count **missed worker hours** when an order fails.
think: A jumpy job flow could leave me with an **empty fortnight**.
Fast tool learning cannot replace **paid local shifts** when few firms hire.
do: Compare an **AI stair order** with the real crate.
Keep **paid fitting shifts** and send error records to the branch.
Apply to **two repair firms** after a one-week start delay.
feel: **Interested and anxious** about a trial funded by workers' lost hours.
S1.quote: I cannot afford a long experiment paid for with my own missing hours.
fieldNote: David asks the buyer for a **real stair trial** and a full record of worker time lost to errors.
His **one-week trigger** follows from a reserve of less than a month and a small local job market.

steps.text: Trial an AI stair order against a delivered crate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the branch that thinking AI in 2028 could take drawings and ordering, while capable site robots arrive about 2031. I would push for paid safety training before a robot works near anyone cutting stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty, I may still have paid fitting work if the sites keep coming. At sixty-three, robots could do the hands-on stair work, and eighteen days saved would barely cover the start of a job search; Paula's wage cannot carry rent alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask the union to seek written robot-safety notice and test a digital stair checker against my own measurements. In 2029 I'll keep taking paid site shifts, apply to the two local maintenance firms if bookings fall, and ask the training centre about a funded placement; I'd enrol only if it pays enough for rent and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the 2031 date, but I am already writing applications and questions. A useful AI skill helps me today and still may not keep my hands employed once robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the training centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named employer, wages during training and a bus route I can actually use. I would not spend our electricity money on a certificate with no paid work behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help bridge the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own bills, and I would rather ask them to proofread an application than pay our rent. The plan needs wages, not goodwill alone.

say: I'd name **2028 thinking work** and the later 2031 site robots.
I'd seek **paid safety training** before a robot joins stair work.
think: At **sixty-three**, robots could take my paid stair fitting.
Our **eighteen-day reserve** and Paula's wage cannot cover a long gap.
do: Seek **written safety notice** and test the digital stair checker.
Keep **paid shifts** in 2029 and apply locally if bookings fall.
Enrol in **funded training** only with wages and reachable work.
feel: **Frightened**, yet actively preparing applications and questions.
S2.quote: A useful AI skill helps me today and still may not keep my hands employed once robots arrive.
fieldNote: He knows daily AI use does not remove the **2031 hands-on risk** to his site wage.
His training interest requires **paid, reachable placement** because the household cannot fund a speculative certificate.

steps.text: Ask the union for written robot-safety notice
Test the digital stair checker against site measurements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should give workers time to test site machines and bargain over wages while training. I would ask the builder to publish a proper list of projects, not just show us a machine at an exhibition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots could repair stairs. More years of pay help only if the site schedule stays full; low rates and lost days may leave us just as short of a retirement cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking South Cut work and use my AI list to record changes between drawings and delivered timber. In 2032 I'd take paid repair jobs if offered, ask the branch for the next six months of project dates and apply to the two local firms if a full week disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less squeezed by the technology timeline, but the household account is still thin. A five-year warning is useful only if it comes with five years of actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you save more in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After a full month I could move a small amount into savings, but I cannot promise that in a month with missing days. Paula and I need to clear the late electricity charge first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would consider a paid trade placement if a reachable employer offered one. I am not enrolling on a promise that a new trade will be safe from robots forever.

say: I'd ask for **published project dates** and paid training terms.
I'd use five years to **test machines** on real site work.
think: At **sixty-six**, site robots may meet a still-thin retirement cushion.
Lost days could erase the benefit of **extra warning**.
do: Keep **paid South Cut work** and checked AI order records.
Apply to **two firms** after another missing week.
feel: Less **pressed by robot dates**, still worried about current money.
S3.quote: A five-year warning is useful only if it comes with five years of actual work.
fieldNote: David's **savings plan** is limited to full paid months after clearing an existing late charge.
He treats a new trade as possible only with a **paid local placement**, not automatic protection.

steps.text: Keep taking paid South Cut and repair shifts in 2032
Use AI to check drawing revisions against timber orders
Ask the union for six months of project dates
Apply to two local firms after a missing week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to teach younger workers how to spot a weak stair and to keep asking who checks a robot's repair. I would also remind the crew that the next pay packet matters before the 2039 machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when site robots follow. I may still need paid repair work then, because today's low wage and tiny reserve give me no sound retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting and repairing timber while paid work is available, and use AI for checked lists that save us time. In 2037 I'd take lighter paid stair repairs if my body allows, and Paula and I would count actual income and bills before I stop applying for shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about robots so far away, but anxious about this winter's site hours. A decade cannot be spent at the grocery counter this Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for public support if work stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the advice office what we qualify for, but I would not assume money arrives until someone confirms it. I'd bring the wage slips and lost-day record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help most now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A firm four-week schedule and one extra paid day each week would let us rebuild savings. I can use every tool in the world, but I still need paid hours.

say: I'd ask who **checks robot repairs** before 2039, especially on stairs that carry families.
I'd remind workers the **next wage packet** comes first.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid repairs may still be necessary.
At **seventy-one**, low wages and thin savings leave retirement uncertain.
do: Keep **paid timber repairs** and checked AI lists.
Take **lighter stair jobs** in 2037 if needed.
Review **income and bills** with Paula before leaving work.
feel: **Anxious about current hours**, calm about distant robot dates.
S4.quote: I can use every tool in the world, but I still need paid hours.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** gives David no permission to assume retirement with current low wages.
He will ask about **verified public support** if work stops, while continuing paid site work where available.

steps.text: Keep taking paid timber repair shifts while fit
Use AI for checked materials lists on paid jobs
Ask the advice office about eligibility only if work stops

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most because robots could reach my stair work by 2031 when Paula and I have almost nothing set aside. Paid local placements, written safety terms and a reliable site schedule would let me keep working through the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who pays for an AI order that sends six workers home early. An AI order that sends six workers home early should include their lost wages in its cost.

headlineQuote: An AI order that sends six workers home early should include their lost wages in its cost.
portrait: David is a **fifty-eight-year-old certified** carpenter with mid-level experience on housing sites.
His low wage, Paula's short hours and **eighteen days saved** make missed work urgent.
He uses **AI every day**, but checks lists against the actual stairs and timber.
He seeks **paid local work**, union records and funded training with wages.
biggestWorry: The **2028 path** could take his stair-fitting wage by 2031 with barely a job-search reserve.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid reachable placements**, written safety terms and reliable site dates.
